h1: The 7 Best Cordless Leaf Blowers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Cordless Leaf Blowers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 cordless leaf blowers from Milwaukee, Ryobi, DEWALT and value brands, compared on listed CFM, battery platform and price.
summary: The Milwaukee M18 FUEL is the best cordless leaf blower for most buyers, pairing 450 CFM and 120 MPH with a brushless motor and a deep battery platform. The RYOBI ONE+ is the pick if your garage already runs on that battery. LOSART and YOOVL list 650 CFM for less money but come with unproven track records. DEWALT's 20V MAX is only for light clean-up.
intro: The trap with cordless blowers is the number on the box. A 650 CFM claim from a brand nobody has heard of and a 450 CFM claim from a major tool platform are not the same promise, even though the digits look like they favor the first one. Airflow figures on budget listings are manufacturer claims, and they rarely come with a battery system you can rely on in three years.

We reviewed seven cordless blowers from their listings and ranked them on listed airflow, air speed, brand support and price tier. Several inexpensive models claim more CFM than the name brands, so we weighed that headline against warranty, replacement batteries and how well each tool fits a normal yard.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 120 MPH 450 CFM 18-Volt Lithium Ion Brushless Blower
products.verdict: A brushless blower on the M18 platform.
products.description:
Milwaukee's M18 FUEL is a brushless 18 volt blower that lists 120 MPH and 450 CFM, in the $100 to $200 price tier. The brushless motor is the part that matters long term, since it runs cooler and wears less than a brushed design.

It leads the ranking because it is the only pick that combines respectable airflow with a platform people actually keep investing in. The budget models below it claim more CFM on paper, but none of them offers a battery family you can add tools to or a brand with established service channels.

Buy it if you already own M18 batteries or want to start a cordless collection around a proven system. The caveat is cost: it asks more than the value brands, and some listings sell the tool without a battery, so confirm what is in the box.

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ 18V 100 MPH 325 CFM Cordless Battery Variable Speed Jet Fan Blower
products.verdict: Variable speed on the huge ONE+ battery system.
products.description:
The RYOBI ONE+ jet fan blower lists 100 MPH and 325 CFM, with a variable speed trigger, and sells in the $100 to $200 tier. It runs on the 18 volt ONE+ battery family, which covers an enormous range of lawn and workshop tools.

Second place comes down to one tradeoff. Its airflow is the lowest of the big-brand blowers here, a clear step under the Milwaukee, yet it asks for the same money. What keeps it high is the ecosystem: if your trimmer and drill already share ONE+ packs, a bare tool is a smart buy.

Buy it if you own Ryobi batteries and your yard is modest. The honest drawback is that someone starting from nothing gets more air for the same budget from the Milwaukee above.
cons: Lowest CFM of the big brands

products.name: LOSART Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A 650 CFM claim in the $50-100 tier.
products.description:
LOSART's cordless blower claims 650 CFM on battery power and sits in the $50 to $100 tier. On paper that is the highest airflow in this ranking, at a price well below the name brands.

Why third rather than first? A listed number is a manufacturer claim, and LOSART has no platform behind it. Replacement batteries, parts and warranty handling are all open questions, which is exactly where a tool from Milwaukee or Ryobi earns its premium. It still beats the cheapest picks below because it advertises substantially more air than MZK or MTKOALA.

Buy it if you want strong stated output on a limited budget and accept some risk. Skip it if you want a battery you can swap into other tools, or the comfort of established support.

products.name: YOOVL Leaf Blower Cordless
products.description:
YOOVL lists the same 650 CFM battery-powered claim as LOSART, in the same $50 to $100 tier. The spec sheets are close to interchangeable, down to the cordless format and the lack of a recognizable platform.

That sameness explains its fourth spot. There is nothing in the listed specs that separates it from LOSART, so it takes the lower slot on ordering alone. It still ranks above MZK and MTKOALA because the claimed airflow is a third higher than their 450 CFM.

Buy it if LOSART is unavailable or priced higher when you shop, since either one fills the same role. The caveat is shared: an unproven brand, an unverified airflow figure and no tool ecosystem to grow into over the years.

products.name: MZK 20V Cordless Leaf Blower
products.verdict: 450 CFM in the lowest price tier here.
products.description:
MZK's 20V cordless blower lists 450 CFM, the same headline number as the Milwaukee, in the $25 to $50 tier. It is the cheapest tool in the ranking by a clear margin.

It lands fifth because price is its entire argument. The claimed airflow trails LOSART and YOOVL, and the brand has little track record to lean on. Against MTKOALA just below, though, it delivers the same listed output for less, which is why it edges ahead.

Buy it if you have a small yard, a patio or a driveway to clear a few times a year and want the lowest entry cost. Skip it if you expect many seasons of service, because replacement packs and support are the uncertain part of any tool at this price.

products.name: MTKOALA 2026 Upgrade Leaf Blower
products.verdict: 450 CFM at a slightly higher price than MZK.
products.description:
MTKOALA's 2026 upgrade blower lists 450 CFM on battery power and sits in the $50 to $100 tier. The spec sheet is short and simple, with no brushless or platform detail to point to.

The problem is the price comparison. MZK lists the same 450 CFM for noticeably less, so MTKOALA has to win on something else, and the listing does not give an obvious reason. It stays above DEWALT because it lists more than four times the airflow, which matters when the job is actually moving leaves.

Buy it if you like its design or find it discounted into MZK territory. Skip it if you want the cheapest option or any kind of established support, since both are better served elsewhere in this list.

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX Blower
products.verdict: A compact 20V MAX blower for existing DEWALT batteries.
products.description:
DEWALT's 20V MAX blower is a compact tool listing 100 CFM, in the $100 to $200 tier. It uses the 20V MAX batteries that fill many DIY toolboxes.

It ranks last for a simple reason: 100 CFM is a fraction of what every other blower here lists, which makes it a poor tool for a lawn full of leaves. The DEWALT name and battery platform earn it respect, but not enough to overcome a gap that large, and it costs far more than the budget models that out-claim it.

Buy it if you already own DEWALT 20V packs and want something light for sweeping a deck, garage or walkway. For actual leaf clearing, the Milwaukee M18 FUEL is the sturdier answer.

methodology.title: Listed airflow
methodology.description: CFM counted as a claim, not a measurement.

methodology.title: Battery platform
methodology.description: Major platforms scored higher for batteries and parts.

whatMatters.detail: Rated in cubic feet per minute, CFM tells you how much air leaves the nozzle, and it largely decides how fast a lawn clears. A higher number helps, but only when the claim is credible. Look for the figure in the listing title or spec table, and compare it against brands of similar standing rather than across the whole page.

Air speed in MPH describes how hard the stream hits, which is what lifts wet leaves and debris stuck in mulch. A blower with big CFM but weak speed can feel soft. The Milwaukee lists 120 MPH and the Ryobi 100 MPH. Check that a listing gives both numbers, not just one.

A battery platform means the same packs power your blower, trimmer and drill, which saves real money since batteries are the costly part. It matters most with the Milwaukee M18 or Ryobi ONE+ picks. Check the battery voltage in the title and whether the listing includes a pack and charger or sells the tool bare.

A brushless motor uses electronics instead of carbon brushes, so it usually runs cooler, wears slower and wastes less battery. That translates to longer life from a given pack. The Milwaukee M18 FUEL is the brushless pick here. Search the bullet points for the word brushless, since listings that have one almost always advertise it.

Brand support decides what happens when a battery fades or a part breaks. Established makers keep packs in stock for years and honor clear warranties, while unknown brands can vanish. This is the main risk with LOSART, YOOVL and MZK. Check the warranty terms on the listing and whether replacement batteries are sold separately.

faq.q: Are cordless leaf blowers strong enough?
faq.a: For most home yards, yes. A blower like the Milwaukee M18 FUEL at 450 CFM clears leaves from a typical lot without trouble. Larger or heavily wooded properties may outgrow cordless output and runtime, which is when a stronger model or a spare battery pack becomes necessary.

Comparing CFM across brands without weighing the platform behind the tool. LOSART and YOOVL list 650 CFM, more than the Milwaukee, but the Milwaukee comes with batteries that fit other tools and a warranty people can rely on years later.

faq.q: Is Milwaukee worth more than LOSART?
faq.a: If you own M18 batteries, yes. The Milwaukee adds a brushless motor, 120 MPH air speed and a platform that keeps paying off. If you have no batteries, LOSART costs less and claims more CFM, but it has no track record behind it.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Charge the battery fully, click on the nozzle and try the speed control before heading outside. The Ryobi ONE+ has a variable trigger, so start low on a hard surface to get a feel for the airflow before clearing a lawn.

Wipe leaves and grass from the air intake after each use and store the battery indoors, away from freezing or extreme heat. On a brushless tool like the Milwaukee M18 FUEL there are no brushes to service, so intake care is nearly everything.

Some do and some do not. Many listings sell the tool bare, so check whether a battery and charger are in the box. This is especially true for platform tools like the Milwaukee or DEWALT 20V MAX, which assume you own packs already.

finalTake: The Milwaukee M18 FUEL is the cordless blower to buy if you want a strong, supported tool that will keep working for years. Ryobi's ONE+ is the sensible choice for existing Ryobi owners. LOSART and YOOVL are tempting for their claimed 650 CFM, but treat that figure as a claim, not a promise. Match the blower to your batteries first, and the brand question mostly answers itself.
